column1: # 1932-D Washington Quarter -- priced ladder
# This file is the SOURCE. `npm run grades` reads it, validates it and writes
# src/data/graded-values.ts, which is committed and is what the site imports.
# Never edit the generated file; edit this one and re-run.
# coin:   the catalogue slug this ladder belongs to
# asof:   the date these rows were read, ISO. Every figure on the site is dated
#         at the figure, and this is that date.
# source: name | url | what it was used for. One per line, at least one needed.
# Columns: grade, low, high, pop, finer, service, sales
#   grade    a slug from GRADES in src/data/grades.ts
#   low/high USD. A range, never a point -- condition dominates within a grade
#            and the sources disagree by more than rounding.
#   pop      certified count AT this grade, blank when nobody published one.
#            BLANK IS NOT ZERO: below the grade where certification pays for
#            itself the census counts almost nothing and means nothing.
#   finer    certified count above this grade
#   service  who counted: PCGS, NGC
#   sales    realized prices, price|month year|house, several joined by ';'
#            Every sale must sit inside low..high -- a range that excludes its
#            own evidence is a page arguing with itself, and the import throws.
# NOT IN THIS LADDER, and each one is the gate working rather than an omission:
# Nothing published names a figure for those rungs on this issue -- the guides
# that quote MS61 quote it inside an MS61-MS62 band, which prices neither. Two
# of them are worth naming:
#   au53  one eBay sale at $208 in June 2018 is on record, below the AU50
#         range from two guides. That is one coin with a problem, not a market.
#   ms61  had a definition written for it and no figure to hang on it, so the
#         rung came back out of GRADES as well. It returns when a sheet prices it.
# A rung needs at least two figures behind it -- a guide value and a realized
# sale each count as one, and a published band counts as its two ends. The low
# is the weakest figure found and the high the strongest, so adjacent ranges
# overlap. That is what the data really looks like at the bottom of this
# ladder, where three grades of a 1932-D trade inside one $70 band, and it is
# the reason the ranges are printed as ranges rather than as points.
